name: Suma
definition: Suma is a composite portrait of a Kuruba woman in Shiggaon taluk, Haveri district, who runs a small tailoring shop from her home while managing household and farm responsibilities. She represents families navigating drought, onion-price crashes, and the gap between government promises and the daily struggle to keep children in school.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Suma wakes before dawn to prepare breakfast and pack tiffin for her husband Basavaraj, who farms three acres of rainfed land half a kilometre from their home in Shiggaon town. After sending her two daughters to school, she opens the small tailoring shop attached to the front room of their house, where she stitches blouses, school uniforms and salwar sets on a pedal machine bought twelve years ago. On good days she earns Rs 200 to Rs 300, but orders drop sharply during the summer months and in years like 2023 and 2026 when the rains fail. Basavaraj grows onion, cotton and jowar; last season the onion price collapsed below Rs 10 per kilo and they could not recover the cost of seed and labour. The household earns perhaps Rs 80,000 in a good year from the farm and another Rs 40,000 from her tailoring, but drought years push them to borrow from the Shiggaon cooperative bank at eighteen per cent or from a private moneylender at two per cent per month. Suma also takes MGNREGA work when it is available, digging farm ponds for Rs 300 a day, though the guarantee of a hundred days is rarely met.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Suma lives with her husband Basavaraj, their daughters Kavya (fifteen, studying in Class 10 at the government high school) and Deepa (twelve, in Class 7), and Basavaraj's widowed mother, who is seventy and receives a Rs 1,000 monthly pension under the Sandhya Suraksha scheme. Suma married at eighteen, soon after finishing Class 10; her parents could not afford to send her further and the family needed one less mouth to feed. She had hoped to study tailoring formally, but learned by watching her aunt. Basavaraj finished PU first year and speaks often of the value of education, insisting both daughters will complete PU and perhaps study further. Kavya is bright and wants to become a nurse, but the family worries about the cost of a nursing course in Haveri or Dharwad—hostel, fees and travel could run to Rs 50,000 a year. Deepa is quieter and enjoys helping her grandmother cook jolada rotti and ennegaai. Suma manages all the cooking, cleaning, washing and caring for her mother-in-law, who has arthritis and cannot walk far. Basavaraj helps with the heavier housework when he is not in the fields, but neighbours expect Suma to do most of it, and she rarely leaves Shiggaon except for the annual Yellamma jatra at Saundatti or a family wedding.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Suma completed SSLC at the Shiggaon government girls' high school in 2004, scoring a second class, and her tailoring skill comes from informal apprenticeship rather than any ITI course. Kavya studies in the Kannada-medium government high school about a kilometre from home; she walks there with friends each morning and returns by two in the afternoon. The school charges no fees under the government scheme, and midday meals are provided, though Kavya says the sambar is often watery and the rice insufficient. Textbooks and uniforms are free, but the family spent Rs 3,000 this year on a geometry box, bags, notebooks, pens and a Rs 500 exam fee for a private coaching class Kavya attends twice a week to prepare for SSLC. Suma worries constantly about whether Kavya will pass—news that Haveri district topped the state in SSLC 2026 with 96.87 per cent brought pride, but also pressure. Suma wishes she had studied more and is determined that her daughters will not face the same limits, though the cost of college and the drought weigh on every conversation about the future.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Suma's mother-in-law suffers from arthritis in both knees and finds it painful to climb stairs or squat for cooking; she takes a painkiller from the Shiggaon government hospital when the pain is severe, but the doctors there have advised surgery at Haveri district hospital, which the family cannot afford. Suma herself has had anaemia since her second pregnancy and was advised to take iron tablets, but she forgets or cannot afford them regularly. She goes to the government hospital for fevers and minor ailments, but serious cases require a trip to Haveri town, twenty-five kilometres away, or even to Hubballi for specialists, which means a day's lost work and Rs 1,000 or more in travel, consultation and medicines. Kavya fainted once during her periods and was found to be anaemic; the school health check-up recommended iron supplements and better food, but Suma struggles to provide eggs or meat more than once a week. The family drinks water from a borewell that Basavaraj suspects has high fluoride—several neighbours have dental fluorosis and joint pain—but testing costs money and the alternative is buying water or boiling it, neither easy. During the summer months the well runs dry and they depend on tanker supply from the gram panchayat, which arrives irregularly. Suma worries about her daughters' health, about the cost of any serious illness, and about her own exhaustion, which she attributes to overwork and the relentless summer heat.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Suma's family belongs to the Kuruba community, a shepherding and farming caste that is listed as OBC in Karnataka; many Kurubas in Haveri district have small or marginal landholdings and depend on rain. The community reveres Kanaka Dasa, the sixteenth-century Haridasa saint, and the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha near Haveri is an important centre of pride and pilgrimage. Suma visits the Peetha once a year with her family, and the mutt has run a free hostel for Kuruba children in Haveri town, though she did not know about it in time for Kavya. The family also goes to the annual Devaragudda Mailara jatra in Haveri district, where thousands gather and the karnika (oracle) delivers prophecies while in trance—Suma finds the atmosphere both frightening and reassuring. They celebrate Ugadi, Deepavali and Sankranti at home with jolada rotti, shenga chutney and jaggery. Suma's husband is devout and often speaks of the Lingayat-Kuruba social closeness, though he also resents that Lingayats dominate local politics and the cooperative society. Neighbours are mostly Kuruba, Lingayat Banajiga and a few Scheduled Caste families; everyone knows everyone and helps during weddings or emergencies, but caste distinctions remain strong and inter-caste marriages are rare. Suma trusts the mutt more than she trusts politicians, and she wishes the Peetha's schools and hostels were closer.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Suma's family has a ration card (BPL until two years ago, now revised to APL because of the land ownership, though their income has not improved), and they receive five kilos of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, which is crucial when cash is short. Suma receives Rs 2,000 per month under Gruha Lakshmi, though the payment has been delayed twice—once for two months in early 2026—and she has heard rumors that the scheme may be revised after the new Chief Minister took office in June 2026. She used the first few instalments to buy a steel cupboard and save a little for Kavya's coaching fees. Basavaraj has tried to register for MGNREGA work but complains that contractors skim wages and the full hundred days are never available; last year he got only thirty-seven days. The family was declared drought-affected in 2023, and they received Rs 4,000 as crop-loss compensation after a taluk officer inspected the fields, though Basavaraj says the loss was much greater. Suma travels to the taluk office in Shiggaon town for certificates or Bhoomi records, and she finds the officials polite but slow; a caste certificate for Kavya's school took four months. She has heard of Kalasa-Banduri and the demand for water from the Mahadayi river, and Basavaraj speaks bitterly about how Kittur Karnataka is ignored while Kalyana Karnataka got Article 371(J) funds and Bengaluru gets everything else.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: She worries most about money—whether the onion crop will fetch a decent price this year, whether the rains will come, whether Kavya will pass SSLC and what it will cost to send her to PU or nursing college. She worries that Deepa, who is quieter, will lose interest in school if the family faces another drought or if neighbours start talking about marriage. Suma blames the government for not protecting farmers from price crashes and for delaying the Mahadayi project, which she has heard could transform Haveri's water situation, but she does not understand why it is taking so long. She blames moneylenders and middlemen for squeezing farmers, and she blames herself for not having studied more or saved more. She is proud of her tailoring, proud that her daughters speak Kannada confidently and study without fear, and proud that her family has never taken a loan from a private moneylender at the worst rates, though they came close last year. She demands better crop prices, reliable water, timely MGNREGA wages, and a government that keeps its promise on Gruha Lakshmi and education costs. She resents that outsiders think North Karnataka is all about Belagavi's border dispute or Hubballi's growth, when most families like hers are simply trying to survive the next drought and keep their children in school.
